prompt: Could you write a captivating short story beginning with the sentence: The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered.
answer:
The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered.

On the morning it was scheduled for demolition, it sneezed.

Mara heard it from her bicycle. A tremendous, dusty *achoo* rattled the boarded windows and sent a pigeon tumbling from the chimney.

She stopped.

“Excuse you,” she said.

The front door opened.

Mara was twelve, which was old enough to recognize a terrible idea and young enough to follow it inside.

The entrance hall smelled of raincoats and burnt toast. Beneath the peeling wallpaper, something moved.

“Hello?”

A ripple traveled along the wall.

Then a voice, faint as a finger drawn through dust, said, “Is it Thursday?”

“Tuesday.”

“Oh.” The floorboards sagged beneath her. “Too soon.”

Outside, a truck reversed with three sharp beeps.

“You know what they’re doing?” Mara asked.

“Yes.”

“Can you walk?”

“Can you?”

“Yes.”

“Lucky.”

She put her bicycle helmet on the banister. Her mother would be furious if she knew where she was. Then again, her mother was furious most mornings now—at misplaced keys, at unopened bills, at the empty chair she still set a cup beside.

“How long have you been able to talk?” Mara asked.

“How long have you been able to listen?”

A man shouted outside. Metal clanged against metal.

“Why didn’t you say anything before?”

“I did. People called it settling.”

Mara pressed her palm against the wall. It was warm.

“Can I help?”

For a while, the only sound was the truck’s engine.

“Under the stairs,” said the house.

There was a small cupboard, and inside it a single red brick resting on a folded towel. Unlike the crumbling bricks outside, this one looked newly fired.

“My first brick,” the house said. “Everything else came afterward.”

Mara lifted it. Something tapped against her fingers.

“Will this save you?”

“I don’t know.”

“What happens to the rest?”

A door clicked open upstairs. Through it she glimpsed yellow curtains stirring in a room without wind.

“I liked being a house,” it said.

The front door shook.

“Anyone in there?”

Mara tucked the brick beneath her coat.

As she reached for her helmet, the banister curled gently around the strap, holding it for one last second.

“Will it hurt?” she whispered.

“I was hoping you knew.”

She went outside.

The demolition man scolded her. She barely heard him. She wheeled her bicycle down the street and didn’t look back when the first wall fell.

That evening, she put the brick beneath her bed.

For six days, nothing happened.

Mara talked to it anyway. She described school, the neighbor’s dog, her mother’s habit of falling asleep with the television on. On the sixth night, she told it about her father.

On the seventh, she woke to the smell of burnt toast.

Her bedroom door, which had always stuck, stood open.

From downstairs came a startled cry.

Mara found her mother in the kitchen, staring at the cupboard beside the stove.

“That handle,” her mother said. “Your dad was going to fix it. I could never get it open.”

It swung outward easily now.

Mara laid a hand against the wall.

Under her palm came a small, familiar warmth.

Her mother sat down. After a moment, she pulled out the chair beside her.

“Tell me about your day,” she said.

And somewhere deep in the walls, very quietly, the house settled.
